@@357684 <p> Dystopia is hardly a novel topic . From H.G. Wells ' " The Time Machine " to Margaret Atwood 's " The Handmaid 's Tale , " society has long had a fascination with alternate realities that are far worse than our own . <p> With the recent scandals stirred up by NSA whistleblower Edward Snowden , the world seems to be becoming more and more Orwellian . Snowden , meanwhile , is becoming a figure much like Katniss Everdeen -- heralded as a hero by some , reviled as a traitor by others . <p> You 'd think that in these times , the popularity of dystopian fiction would plummet , that readers would want their fantasy escapes to be just that -- fantastical and whimsical -- not nightmarish versions of their own reality . Go to any bookstore , however , and take a look around ; in the Young Adult department in particular , dystopian novels dominate the shelves . <p> Suzanne Collins ' " The Hunger Games " is a wildly popular series ( and current blockbuster franchise , although these days the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ darkest to ever gain mainstream appeal among teenagers . The final book was bleaker and more disturbing than many adult novels . Beloved characters die graphic deaths , and the characters who do survive ( spoiler alert , although I do n't feel too bad because the third book came out awhile ago ) are too entrapped by grief , PTSD , and alcoholism to make the " happy ending " feel anything other than hollow . <p> I 'm not criticizing the direction that Collins decided to take with the series . ( Although I will take the opportunity to say that the death of a certain character whose name begins with " F " was Red Wedding-levels of cruel and unnecessary ) . I 'm simply posing the question : What 's behind the surge of dystopian novels in the Young Adult department ? In other words , why are nightmarish , futuristic alternate-realities suddenly sexy ? <p> One reason is , of course , that authors are jumping aboard the " Hunger Games " bandwagon -- Suzanne Collins made good money , so it 's tempting to cash @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ novels gained success even before " The Hunger Games " -- Neal Shusterman 's hauntingly brilliant " Unwind " comes to mind . " Unwind " has a vaguely similar premise to Kazuo Ishhiguro 's " Never Let Me Go . " ( the latter is a quieter story with passive characters , while the former has a simpler style , with protagonists who never stop fighting and transgressing ) . <p> The difference between books like " Unwind " and books capitalizing on the " Hunger Games " trend is that the former explores and develops every aspect of its invented world , from the minute details to the big picture . Many authors seem to think that the prime ingredient of a dystopia is a clever premise , typically involving destruction , oppressive societies , and love triangles . Along the way , many authors forget to develop their own worlds beyond a single facet of their premise . <p> Ally Condie 's " Matched , " for example , focuses on the love triangle , while Kimberly Derting 's " The Plege " focuses on societal oppression to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ all but the vaguest understanding of the society itself . <p> Carrie Ryan 's " The Forest of Hands and Teeth " draws so much on destruction ( in this case , a zombie outbreak ) that she forgets to give her characters -- well , character . Justin Cronin 's " The Passage " has the opposite problem , with such enormous scope that he ca n't pull the corners of his vast universe together to create a coherent narrative . <p> In dystopian fiction , what differentiates the intriguing from the incoherent is that in the former , the nightmarish world is convincing and plausible . The book itself does n't have to be pleasing by conventional standards : Margaret Atwood , for example , is a brilliant writer , but " The Handmaid 's Tale " ( the weakest of her books ; if you want to read her best , opt for " The Blind Assassin " ) is not conventionally " good , " possessing no ending . Nevertheless , her world is fully realized and developed . <p> Other examples of teen dystopia with well-developed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ creative take on materialism , Tanith Lee 's " The Claidi Journals , " where quirky steampunk meets Arabian nights , and Meg Rosoff 's " How I Live Now , " a darkly hypnotic , harrowing war story . Finally , Stephanie Meyer ( the same woman responsible for polarizing the vampire genre and offering shining contributions to the film genre of " unintentionally hilarious " ) has a shockingly good addition to the list with " The Host . " <p> Does the popularity of dystopia fiction then mean that teenager 's tastes are growing darker ? <p> As an adult who still unabashedly reads dystopian young adult novels ( I 'd say it 's a guilty pleasure but I do n't feel too guilty about it ; many are damn good stories ) I 'd have to say there 's more to it than that . The popularity of certain kinds of fiction directly relates to reality -- and the allure of fiction has always had roots in escapism . Therefore , as our own reality becomes darker , we turn to fiction for escape . Dystopian novels @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ may be bad , but at least it 's not that bad ! " <p> Dystopian realities tend to come with incredibly high stakes . Government oppression and corruption is a common trope , as well as wars , forced conformity , religious fanaticism , and heroes facing odds that are incredible to the point of hopelessness . Most of all , they feature heroes fighting against those odds . Dystopian heroes typically suffer more than ordinary heroes , and not all of them make it out alive , but they all put up a fight . <p> So , is it any wonder that , in our world today , where people feel powerless , popular fiction has taken a darker turn ? And , if you 're wondering why dystopian novels line the Teen shelves in particular -- well , your teenage years are when you automatically feel the most powerless . <p> In a world where we feel watched and monitored , in a world where school shootings abound and the people who are supposed to be in charge do n't seem to be doing anything to monitor @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in power still deny that climate change is a problem , where our own reality often seems like something George Orwell or Ray Bradbury would conjure -- is it any wonder that our popular , sexy escapism has become nightmarish speculations of the future ? 
@@357923 <h> Can The Threat Of Climate Change Make Cities Richer And Healthier ? <p> If cities are trying to reduce their footprint and investing in a climate-proof infrastructure , the benefits are astounding . <p> Climate change , we 're told , is a scary thing . There 's nothing but floods , droughts , hurricanes , fires , and heat waves for us to look forward to . Superstorm Sandy was a mere preview of that future -- the kind of thing we can expect to happen much more frequently down the line . So you can imagine my surprise upon seeing this phrase emblazoned across the top of a report from the Carbon Disclosure Project : " How climate change action is giving us wealthier , healthier cities . " <p> It 's not that climate change itself is making cities richer and healthier , the CDP postulates . But all the preparations they 're making -- like emissions reductions and energy efficiency -- are creating more walkable and bikeable neighborhoods , attracting investments , and cutting costs . <p> The benefit of taking action on @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ reducing emissions . <p> The report analyzed data from members of the C40 Cities Climate Leadership Group in 110 cities around the world , including Tokyo , New York , and London . The CDP 's main conclusion : <p> The data from these cities makes clear that the benefit of taking action on climate change at the city level is not limited to reducing emissions or adapting to warmer temperatures . The cities in the survey are engaged on the issue of climate change , and , as a result , are saving money , creating more attractive investment environments , and enabling citizens to live healthier lives . In short , climate change action by local governments around the world is creating wealthier , healthier cities . <p> Energy efficiency measures are by far the most popular actions that cities are taking to cut down on CO2 emissions -- mainly by cutting down on energy demand in buildings , boosting municipal fleet fuel efficiency , and reducing both energy consumption maintenance costs of outdoor lighting . <p> These three actions make up 25% of everything that cities are doing @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Washington , D.C. , a plan to retrofit thousands of residential building units owned by the D.C. Housing Authority ( 5,400 units have been retrofitted so far ) has yielded $3.9 million in electricity savings each year along with $2.4 million in operations and maintenance savings -- not to mention the energy bill savings for residents . <p> The report also suggests that taking emissions reduction actions can be attractive to businesses . After analyzing all 800 actions that the surveyed cities are taking , here 's what the CDP has deemed the best for business ( based on academic research on whether they lead to economic growth ) : <p> According to the report , cities strongly believe ( 91% of respondents ) that taking action on climate change will make them better places to invest . CDP points out places where this is already happening : In Detroit , for example , a renewed interest in cycling has led to the growth of the bicycle manufacturing industry . <p> Cities are also tackling the potential health consequences of climate change -- things like cholera from flooding and general increased @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ approaches based on the threats they face . Mexico City is dealing with heat waves by implementing better epidemiological monitoring , which has found that poorly preserved street food left out in the heat is giving people stomach issues . Cape Town is confronting its flooding-related health risks by outlining " no-development " areas , keeping a strong stormwater runoff infrastructure , and doing coastal vulnerability mapping . <p> All of these actions are unquestionably making certain cities more attractive to investors and residents . And they 're saving lots of money . But eventually , even the best-prepared cities will be hit by climate-related disasters that cost many millions , if not billions , of dollars . The prepared cities will be wealthier and healthier than areas that failed to do anything , but they 'll still suffer . In the short term , though , it 's accurate to say that the threat of climate change is triggering cities to take actions that save money , make life more pleasant for residents , and cut down on emissions . 
@@358092 <p> Climate change seems like this complicated problem with a million pieces . But Henry Jacoby , an economist at MIT 's business school , says there 's really just one thing you need to do to solve the problem : Tax carbon emissions . <p> " If you let the economists write the legislation , " Jacoby says , " it could be quite simple . " He says he could fit the whole bill on one page . <p> Basically , Jacoby would tax fossil fuels in proportion to the amount of carbon they release . That 's it ; that 's the whole plan . <p> Jacoby 's colleague John Reilly told me the price of gasoline might rise by 25 cents a gallon in the first year . Over time , that would increase . By 2050 , Reilly figures the carbon tax would add about $1 to the price of every gallon . Across the economy , prices of energy-intensive goods and services would rise . This would encourage people and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ economists love a carbon tax : One change to the tax code and the entire economy shifts to reduce carbon emissions . No complicated regulations . No rules for what kind of gas mileage cars have to get or what specific fraction of electricity has to come from wind or solar or renewables . That 's by and large the way we do it now . <p> Reilly says the current web of rules is a more complicated and more expensive way of getting the same outcome as a carbon tax . @@361236 <p> Provocative , if not entirely convincing , Denial has a doozy of a premise : The key factor that makes humans human is a highly developed ability to deny reality . <p> The book got its start from a conversation in 2005 between geneticist Danny Brower and biomedical researcher Ajit Varki . When Brower died in 2007 , he left behind the draft of a book on the subject . With the permission of Brower 's widow , Varki revised and expanded the manuscript . <p> The idea is that humans are the only animals who have developed a " full theory of mind . " In other words , humans are not only self-aware -- a trait shared to some extent with other species -- but also aware that other beings are self-aware and share the same feelings and consciousness they have . <p> The downside of this , the authors contend , is that , if you recognize that someone is like you and you see that person die , you will suddenly realize that you , too , are going to die . The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ depression and paralyzing behavior " that those afflicted with the knowledge not only would be unlikely to reproduce but also might commit suicide . <p> Only those who almost simultaneously made the psychological leap into denial of mortality would go on to propagate the species . Brower and Varki argue that this is indeed what happened to a small group of humans who then went on to become the ancestors of all of us . <p> It 's hard not to be skeptical about the notion of cave-man Woody Allens brooding while their less intelligent , or at least more deluded , brethren cavorted about blissfully if ignorantly spreading their genetic material . <p> The notion that denial is key to the human psyche is intriguing -- but it could also be argued that one man 's denial is another man 's faith . <p> When the authors write about " denial of reality , " they have a specific , narrow view of reality in mind . <p> " We now know that reality as revealed by science is in fact the real truth , " they say , without @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ half of the book goes off on the tangent of describing the many ways in which the authors think humans deny reality : They do n't recognize the reality of climate change ; they smoke when they know smoking is bad for their health ; they sky-dive and eat red meat . <p> Much of this seems more related to the trade-off between present pleasures and future rewards than to the type of deep-seated psychological denial the authors propose is wired into us . <p> At its heart , the book is another volley in the ongoing war between optimists and pessimists , with the pessimists overcoming their brains ' hard-wiring to remind their fellow species members to be " terrified and depressed by the fact that you are just the tiniest little transient blip in this enormous reality of time and space . "
